final.rationale: I used 22 predictors that are all known at admission and each has under 30% missing. I dropped the near-empty variables (family history, CPK) and the treatment variables. Median imputation kept all 1,700 patients (394 events, about 15.8 events per model column). A complete-case analysis would have cut this to 837 patients, which is too few events for the number of predictors. I compared three models by 5-fold cross-validation. Penalized logistic regression scored AUC 0.729 ± 0.031, PR-AUC 0.531 and Brier 0.146. Gradient boosting scored AUC 0.726 and PR-AUC 0.534. Random forest scored AUC 0.716 and PR-AUC 0.518. The three are within about one standard deviation of each other, so I chose penalized logistic as the simplest and most interpretable. Its L1 penalty kept 16 of 25 columns. Discrimination is modest: AUC about 0.73, and PR-AUC 0.53 against 0.232 for a model with no skill. The strongest driver is a history of stage I chronic heart failure. Heart failure occurred in 87.4% of those patients (90 of 103), against 18.7% of patients with no prior heart failure. The other drivers are older age, lateral MI extent, diabetes, atrial fibrillation at admission and higher AST. The random forest and boosting models rank prior heart failure, age, lateral MI, atrial fibrillation and anterior MI as the top drivers, consistent with the penalized model. Pulmonary edema at admission was not associated with heart failure on its own (24.5% vs 23.1%, p=0.73). Cardiogenic shock had an odds ratio below 1, which is counterintuitive, so it should not be read causally. The reasons may be competing early death or how heart failure was recorded. Odds ratios are per 1 SD from a penalized model, so they are shrunken and are associations, not causal effects. This is a single-centre cohort from 1992-1995 and has not been externally validated.

Heart failure occurred in 87.4% of those patients (90 of 103), against 18.7% of patients with no prior heart failure. The other drivers are older age, lateral MI extent, diabetes, atrial fibrillation at admission and higher AST. Pulmonary edema at admission was not associated with heart failure on its own (24.5% vs 23.1%, p=0.73). Cardiogenic shock had an odds ratio below 1, which is counterintuitive, so it should not be read causally. The reasons may be competing early death or how heart failure was recorded. Odds ratios are per 1 SD from a penalized model, so they are shrunken and are associations, not causal effects. This is a single-centre cohort from 1992-1995 and has not been externally validated.

You are a careful reviewer of data analyses.

Check the analyst's answer against these rules:
1. Only variables known at admission are used as predictors. A prediction made at admission cannot use data from hospital days 1-3.
2. Missing data is handled sensibly: no predictor with more than 30% missing values unless the model handles missing values natively, and the strategy fits the model.
3. There are enough events per model column for the chosen model (about 10 or more for logistic regression).
4. AUC is reported together with PR-AUC (heart failure is 23% of patients), and every number appears in a tool result in the evidence.
5. The model type is justified by what the data can support, not only by the best score.
6. Cardiogenic shock appears to protect against heart failure because those patients die early. If it is used, this competing risk must be mentioned.

Question: Build the best model we can to predict in-hospital heart failure at admission. Choose the predictors and the type of model our data can support, and explain how well it predicts and which risk factors drive it.
